review.material: Primary paper: definitions in §2, both exercises in §3, and conclusions; selected illustrated constructions.
review.limitations: The central framework and both exercises were reviewed. The many illustrated rule variants were sampled rather than exhaustively checked.

evidence.locator: pp. 188–194, §2: shape, spatial relations and grammars
evidence.description: The formal vocabulary for recurring geometric arrangements.
Constructing languages from a chosen vocabulary and edge relations.
Inferring grammars from an existing arrangement and its possible decompositions.

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Two complementary exercises show how to explore families of shapes: start with elements and allowable relations, or start with a drawing and infer rules that generate it and related drawings.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: How can formal composition be investigated systematically while retaining a direct visual connection between rules and the shapes they produce?

sections.title: Main idea or claim
sections.text: Shape grammars make recurring spatial relations explicit. Different choices of vocabulary, relations and decomposition can define different languages, even when they begin with the same visible example.

sections.title: How the work approaches it
sections.text: Exercise 1 chooses polygons, enumerates ways they can share an edge, and turns these relations into recursive rules. Exercise 2 decomposes an existing polygon arrangement, extracts relations, and constructs grammars that also produce further arrangements.

sections.title: Evidence and examples
sections.text: Polygon and triangle constructions illustrate rule variants and finite or infinite generated families. One shape is read as five squares or as two L-shaped components, showing why parsing affects the inferred grammar.

sections.title: What comes out of it
sections.text: A compact rule system can describe both an existing example and a larger family. Recursion supplies constructive explanations of form, rather than only a catalogue of completed drawings.

sections.title: Limits to keep in mind
sections.text: The paper calls the exercises suggestive. Its common-grammar account of style is a modeling assumption, not an empirical test of historical style or proof that functional design requirements are satisfied.

sections.title: What to take from it
sections.text: Try both directions: generate from relations, then infer alternative relations from a result. Compare the languages each choice permits instead of assuming one decomposition is definitive.
